De methode is in hoofdlijnen coherent en sluit aan op de onderzoeksvraag en hypothese. De deelnemers, inclusie- en exclusiecriteria, randomisatie, condities, hoofdmeetinstrument en globale procedure zijn aanwezig. Ook is de vergelijking tussen CGT+VRET en CGT+in vivo in de kern begrijpelijk en passend bij het beoogde design.

Er ontbreken echter meerdere details die volgens de schrijfwijzer belangrijk zijn. Bij de participanten is de groepsverdeling qua gender in de tekst inconsistent met de latere tabel. De leeftijdsrange in de tekst is 13-19 jaar, maar de gemiddelde leeftijden in de tabel liggen rond 17 en de eerdere introductie focust sterk op adolescenten zonder nadere afbakening. De materialenbeschrijving is deels te globaal voor replicatie: de opbouw van de acht sessies, standaardisatie tussen condities, precieze verschillen tussen VRET en in vivo, en hoe exposure-intensiteit systematisch werd bepaald, blijven onvoldoende uitgewerkt. Ook staat in de materialen dat deelnemers angst rapporteerden via LSAS-CA-scores, terwijl de LSAS-CA eerder als uitkomstmaat op T0, T1 en T2 beschreven wordt; dat schept verwarring tussen behandelmonitoring en afhankelijke variabele. Verder ontbreekt een echte analyseparagraaf en blijft onduidelijk hoe missing data of uitval op 12 maanden zijn behandeld.

Dit komt uit op Adequate: het design is coherent en grotendeels passend, maar er missen meer dan één of twee details die voor volledigheid en reproduceerbaarheid relevant zijn.
methods_rubric_feedback: De methoderubriek is helder in haar nadruk op coherentie, volledigheid en plaatsing van informatie. Een mogelijke verbetering is om de bands specifieker te koppelen aan de vereiste subonderdelen uit de schrijfwijzer, zoals allocation, beloning, inclusie/exclusie, operationalisatie van DVs, en analyseplan. Nu blijft het soms lastig om precies te bepalen wanneer ontbrekende details nog 'één of twee belangrijke details' zijn versus 'multiple important details'. Meer concrete ankers zouden de interbeoordelaarsbetrouwbaarheid verhogen.
results_feedback:
De resultaten volgen deels de verwachte structuur: er is een korte inleiding, er worden assumpties genoemd, er wordt een mixed ANOVA gerapporteerd, en er wordt verwezen naar tabellen en een figuur. Daarmee zijn de basiselementen herkenbaar aanwezig.

Toch is de sectie duidelijk onder het niveau van een gemiddelde voldoende-plus volgens het voorbeeld. Er ontbreken cruciale statistische details: de vrijheidsgraden zijn niet ingevuld bij alle F-toetsen, de tabellen zelf zijn onvolledig weergegeven, en de descriptieve statistiek is niet netjes en volledig uitgewerkt in tabelvorm zoals gevraagd. Ook is er een duidelijke inconsistentie tussen de methode en de resultaten: in de methode is sprake van een 12-maanden follow-up, maar in de tekst staat ook 'drie maanden follow-up'. De interpretatie van de uitkomsten is bovendien intern tegenstrijdig. In de resultaten wordt gezegd dat CGT+in vivo tussen post en follow-up verder daalt terwijl VRET stabiel blijft, maar de discussie stelt elders dat de daling van VRET+CGT over pre naar follow-up groter is dan die van CGT+in vivo. Op basis van de losse gemiddelden onderaan lijkt juist VRET op follow-up lager dan in vivo, maar omdat de tabellen onvolledig en slecht geformatteerd zijn, blijft dat moeilijk controleerbaar. Daarnaast is de rapportage van p-waarden onjuist geformuleerd op meerdere plekken (bijv. 'p = < .001').

Volgens de rubric is dit net voldoende binnen Developing: de gekozen analyse is relevant en deels correct, maar de rapportage is onvolledig en op meerdere punten incoherent ten opzichte van design en eigen tekst.
results_rubric_feedback: De resultatenrubriek profiteert van de koppeling aan het sample results document; dat geeft studenten en beoordelaars een concreet referentiepunt. Wel is de rubric relatief breed geformuleerd. Het zou helpen om minimale vereisten expliciet als checklist op te nemen, bijvoorbeeld: demografietabel, tabel met descriptives per conditie/tijd, assumpties, omnibus test met dfs en p-waarden, post-hocs, en figuur. Ook zou verduidelijkt kunnen worden hoe zwaar interne inconsistenties tussen tabellen, tekst en discussie moeten wegen ten opzichte van louter ontbrekende APA/statistiekdetails.
discussion_feedback:
De discussie opent met een duidelijke terugkoppeling naar doel, onderzoeksvraag en hypothese. Er wordt onderscheid gemaakt tussen korte- en langetermijnbevindingen, en er is een poging om resultaten te verbinden aan eerdere studies en aan de twee theoretische kaders. Ook bevat de sectie studie-specifieke beperkingen, suggesties voor vervolgonderzoek en maatschappelijke implicaties. Dat zijn duidelijke sterke punten.

De kwaliteit van de redenering is echter wisselend. Het grootste probleem is dat de bespreking niet altijd consistent is met de gerapporteerde resultaten. De discussie bevat tegenstrijdige uitspraken over welk conditieverschil op follow-up precies gevonden werd en wat dat betekent voor de hypothese. Daardoor wordt de hoofdconclusie minder overtuigend. Verder worden sommige interpretaties te stellig gepresenteerd, terwijl de resultaten en opzet daar eigenlijk terughoudender formulering vragen. De koppeling aan eerdere literatuur is aanwezig, maar soms wat selectief of onnauwkeurig. Ook de theoretische implicaties blijven redelijk algemeen; de theorieën worden wel genoemd, maar niet heel precies uitgewerkt in termen van welke onderdelen van de theorie nu wel of niet door de bevindingen zijn ondersteund.

Daarmee past deze discussie het best in Adequate/laag Good, maar door de interne inconsistenties valt zij het meest overtuigend in Adequate: grotendeels correct en relevant, met studie-specifieke reflectie, maar niet overal coherent of sterk uitgewerkt.
discussion_rubric_feedback: De discussierubriek sluit goed aan bij wetenschappelijk redeneren doordat zij niet alleen conclusie en beperkingen beoordeelt, maar ook de koppeling aan theorie en eerdere literatuur. Een nuttige aanscherping zou zijn om explicieter te benoemen dat interne consistentie met de eigen Results essentieel is. Daarnaast zou de rubric kunnen specificeren dat theoretische implicaties meer zijn dan alleen theorie noemen: het gaat om aangeven welke theoretische verwachtingen wel, niet of gedeeltelijk ondersteund zijn. Dat onderscheid zou vooral helpen tussen Adequate en Good.
lang_style_feedback:
De tekst is over het algemeen leesbaar en de globale structuur van een wetenschappelijk artikel is goed herkenbaar. De meeste paragrafen hebben een duidelijk onderwerp en de gebruikte terminologie is meestal voldoende consistent om de lijn te volgen. Dat ondersteunt een voldoende voor taal en stijl.

Er zijn echter vrij veel fouten en slordigheden die de professionele afwerking beperken. Voorbeelden zijn grammaticale fouten, onhandige formuleringen, inconsequente termgebruik (bijv. VRET+CGT vs. CGT+VRET), typefouten, spatiefouten en meerdere APA-onregelmatigheden in de referenties en in-text citations. Ook zijn sommige zinnen omslachtig of semantisch onduidelijk. In de resultaten en tabellen is de vormgeving duidelijk zwak, wat de helderheid verlaagt. De taal belemmert het begrip niet voortdurend, maar er zijn wel genoeg fouten en inconsistenties om onder het niveau van 'satisfactory and clear' uit de adequate band te blijven.

Daarom past een beoordeling in Developing het best.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: De taal- en stijlrubriek is bruikbaar doordat zij duidelijk maakt dat taal alleen hier zwaar meeweegt en niet automatisch andere secties omlaag trekt. Dat is didactisch sterk. Tegelijk zijn de drempels vrij foutentellend geformuleerd (bijv. aantal APA- of grammaticafouten), wat in de praktijk lastig eenduidig toe te passen is. Meer nadruk op effect op leesbaarheid en consistentie, met minder nadruk op exact tellen, zou de rubric waarschijnlijk robuuster maken. Ook kan overwogen worden om tabel- en figuuropmaak explicieter onder deze categorie te noemen.

intro_feedback: The introduction contains the major required components: societal relevance appears early, key concepts are defined, the required core studies are discussed, an additional article is included, and the research question and hypothesis are explicitly stated. The overall line of reasoning is generally understandable and mostly leads toward the proposed comparison between CGT+VRET and CGT+in vivo in adolescents. A strength is that the student clearly identifies the adolescent population as a gap in the literature and links that gap to the long-term design. However, the argumentation is only partly synthesized. Several paragraphs still read more like sequential article summaries than like tightly connected building blocks. The theoretical framework is present, but the link between theory and the specific prediction that VRET+CGT should outperform CGT+in vivo on the long term is not fully convincing, especially because the explanation of why the combination should be more durable remains somewhat assertive. There are also some inaccuracies or overstatements in how prior studies are characterized. Overall this fits the adequate band: sound and mostly coherent, with some synthesis, but not yet consistently strong or fully convincing.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric is strong in emphasizing argumentative coherence and the need to build toward the research question rather than merely summarize studies. A useful improvement would be to make the required balance between theory, prior research synthesis, and explicit design justification even more operational. For example, the rubric could specify what counts as adequate synthesis versus sequential summary more concretely. It may also help to distinguish more clearly between minor factual inaccuracies in describing studies and deeper flaws in argumentative reasoning, since both can currently end up affecting the same criterion.
methods_feedback: The methods section describes a coherent randomized design that matches the stated research question reasonably well. Participants, inclusion and exclusion criteria, recruitment, randomization, interventions, primary outcome measure, and measurement moments are all present. This makes the study broadly understandable and partially replicable at this level. The main weaknesses are missing or underdeveloped details that the writing guide expects. Allocation is mentioned, but the randomization procedure itself is not explained. The materials section gives a useful overview of the interventions, yet standardization across conditions is not fully specified, and the description of the treatment protocol is somewhat compressed. The questionnaire description includes several required details, but not all elements are consistently complete or precise. The procedure is quite brief and omits chronological detail about what participants experienced session by session, duration of assessments, consent/debriefing, and how follow-up was arranged. There is also some mixing of material and procedure language. These issues lower the score, but the design remains coherent and aligned with the hypotheses, so the section remains in the adequate range.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric appropriately prioritizes coherence, completeness, and alignment with the research question rather than perfection. It would benefit from more explicit anchors for common student-level omissions, such as missing randomization detail, underdeveloped procedure chronology, or incomplete questionnaire descriptions. Right now, deciding whether something is 'one or two important details' versus 'multiple important details' can be subjective. Adding a short checklist tied to the writing guide could improve consistency between graders.
results_feedback: The results section includes the expected broad components: reference to demographics, a mixed ANOVA, assumption checks, interaction interpretation, post-hoc comparisons, and a figure/table structure. However, the reporting is incomplete in several important ways relative to the sample and rubric. The tables themselves are not properly reproduced in the section text, and crucial descriptive information is therefore only partially available. Test statistics are missing degrees of freedom for all reported F-tests, making the inferential reporting incomplete. Assumption checks are described too vaguely, with no concrete test values except a Greenhouse-Geisser estimate, and the wording is not always statistically precise. There is also inconsistency in the timing language: the design specifies a 12-month follow-up, but the results at one point refer to a three-month follow-up. Some p-value formatting is incorrect, and the post-hoc reporting is not fully systematic. Most importantly, the reporting is understandable but not complete enough to meet the sample-based expectation of this assignment. Because the analysis remains relevant to the design and a basic pattern can still be followed, this fits the developing range rather than insufficient.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric is helpful because it anchors expectations to the sample results section. A potential refinement would be to specify which missing elements are most serious, for example absent descriptive tables, missing degrees of freedom, missing post-hoc tests, or inconsistent reporting of the follow-up interval. That would make it easier to distinguish between developing and adequate performance. It may also help to clarify how much statistical imprecision can be tolerated when the intended analysis and interpretation are otherwise correct.
discussion_feedback: The discussion has a clear opening paragraph that restates the aim, summarizes the findings, and indicates which parts of the hypothesis were supported. The student also attempts to interpret the results in relation to previous studies and to the theoretical framework, and the discussion includes study-specific limitations, future research directions, and broader implications. These are all positive elements. The main limitation is the internal coherence of the interpretation. The student notices the unexpected long-term pattern, which is good, but the interpretation of the overall pattern is sometimes contradictory. For example, the text states that only the in vivo condition continued improving from post to follow-up, yet later still concludes that VRET+CGT is the more valuable treatment overall. That conclusion is not always fully justified by the reported long-term findings. Some comparisons to prior literature are also somewhat overstated or not entirely accurate. The theory links are present, especially to Emotional Processing Theory and Inhibitory Learning Theory, but they are used somewhat broadly rather than in a tightly evidence-based way. The limitations are more specific than generic and the future directions follow reasonably from them. Overall, this is mostly complete and mostly coherent, but not consistently well argued enough for the good band.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric usefully emphasizes interpretation, linkage to theory, and study-specific critical reflection. A refinement could be to more explicitly separate three dimensions within the discussion: accuracy of conclusion from the actual results, integration with prior literature, and quality of limitations/future directions. At present these can blend together, which may reduce inter-rater consistency. It would also help if the rubric more clearly signaled how to grade discussions that engage with theory but do so in a broad or somewhat speculative way.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally readable and the scientific tone is mostly appropriate for this level. The structure across sections is visible, and terminology is usually understandable. However, there are enough language and style issues to lower the score. There are recurring grammar and phrasing problems, punctuation inconsistencies, capitalization inconsistencies, and APA/reference errors. Some sentences are awkward or imprecise, and a few statements are ambiguous or too absolute. Terminology is not always fully consistent, for example in naming conditions and follow-up timing. There is also some redundancy, especially in the discussion where similar claims are repeated. These issues do not usually block understanding, but they are frequent enough that the section fits better in the developing range than in the adequate range.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is detailed and practical, especially in protecting content grades from being overly influenced by minor language issues. One possible improvement is to define the distinction between 'different errors' and repeated versions of the same error more clearly, as this can be difficult to apply consistently. It may also help to separate APA formatting from general readability a little more explicitly, since a paper can be readable but weak in reference formatting, or vice versa.

intro_feedback: The Introduction presents a clear topic, establishes societal relevance, defines key concepts, and ends with a clear research aim and hypothesis. The student also attempts to build a theoretical rationale around self-efficacy and uses prior literature to motivate the comparison between self-guided and therapist-guided VRET. This makes the overall line of reasoning understandable and relevant. However, the argument is only somewhat convincing rather than strong. The literature review is more summary-based than synthesizing, and the required core studies are not always integrated accurately into the argument. There are also some conceptual inconsistencies, for example in how prior studies are characterized and how confidently self-efficacy is used to predict superiority of self-guided VRET without directly measuring self-efficacy. The transition to the research question is present, but the logic could be tighter and the design-specific gap could be argued more explicitly. Overall this fits an adequate/average Introduction.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric captures the importance of coherence, relevance, and responsible use of references well, but it could be improved by distinguishing more explicitly between summary of literature and actual synthesis of literature. At present, students can appear to meet the criterion with a sequence of article summaries even when the argumentative build-up is weak. It may also help to specify that the theoretical framework should not only be present but should be clearly tied to the hypothesis and later discussion.
methods_feedback: The Methods section describes a coherent three-group design that is related to the research question and hypothesis. Participants, broad recruitment approach, inclusion criteria, compensation, intervention conditions, and the planned analysis are all mentioned. At the same time, several details that are important according to the writing guide are missing or underdeveloped. The participant description lacks full sample characteristics beyond age and gender table information placed later; exclusion criteria are not fully justified; allocation is described informally as 'AI (coinflip)', which is not an appropriate scientific description of randomization. The materials section is incomplete for the LSAS because response format, score range, example item, and scoring details are not fully reported. The procedure also leaves important ambiguities, such as when and where pre/post assessments were administered and how adherence was monitored in the self-guided condition. A larger issue is comparability of the two treatment conditions: the self-guided condition involved daily sessions across 14 days, while the therapist-guided condition involved four sessions, making the manipulation less well controlled. So the section is coherent but only nearly complete and only mostly correct.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric appropriately emphasizes coherence with the research question and completeness of participants, materials, and procedure. A useful refinement would be to spell out more concretely what 'complete and correct' means at this student level, for example requiring allocation procedure, inclusion/exclusion criteria, basic instrument details, and enough intervention detail for rough replication. This would make grading more consistent across assessors.
results_feedback: The Results section follows the expected overall structure at a basic level: it includes a demographics table, an outcome table, identifies the main analysis, and reports the general pattern. However, the reporting is substantially incomplete and statistically inconsistent. The ANOVA statistics are not reported in acceptable form: the F-values and degrees of freedom appear implausible or malformed, p-values are incompletely formatted, and key assumption checks are too limited. The section refers to Table 1, Table 2, and Figure 1, but in the body of the paper these are not properly integrated in a polished results narrative. There is also an important inconsistency where the text first states that the post-measurement difference was significant with therapist-guided VRET showing the biggest reduction, but then says there was no significant difference between self-guided and therapist-guided VRET at post-assessment. In addition, one sentence incorrectly refers to PCL-5 scores instead of LSAS scores, suggesting reporting was not carefully adapted to this study. The wait-list group is underreported in the inferential results. Because the general intended analysis matches the design but the reporting is incomplete and partly incoherent, this section is just at the passing threshold.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric gives a sensible progression from incorrect/incomplete to correct/complete, but it remains somewhat broad. Because this course provides a sample Results section, the rubric could benefit from explicit anchors such as presence of demographic table, descriptive statistics table, match between analysis and design, reporting of assumptions, and clear post-hoc interpretation. That would better align the rubric with the sample and reduce ambiguity in borderline cases.
discussion_feedback: The Discussion clearly restates the aim, summarizes the key findings, and directly addresses whether the hypothesis was supported. It correctly notes that both treatment conditions reduced social anxiety symptoms and that the prediction of self-guided superiority was not supported. The student also makes a reasonable attempt to interpret the null difference by considering benefits of therapist guidance and links this explanation to outside literature. Limitations and future research are included and are relevant rather than purely generic. However, the discussion is not fully developed. The integration with the theoretical framework remains fairly surface-level: self-efficacy is discussed as an explanatory idea, but because it was not measured, the conclusions about mechanism remain speculative and this is not critically examined enough. The wait-list condition is mentioned in the conclusion but not deeply discussed in the main discussion. Theoretical implications and broader societal implications are present only briefly. Overall, though, the reasoning is mostly coherent and relevant, fitting an adequate score.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric correctly prioritizes the reasoning leading to the main conclusion and the relevance of the critical reflection. It could be strengthened by explicitly mentioning interpretation of findings in relation to both prior literature and the paper's own theoretical framework, because students may otherwise provide a conclusion and generic limitations without truly engaging in scientific argumentation. Adding a clearer criterion for implications that follow from the actual findings would also improve precision.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally readable and the scientific register is mostly appropriate for this course level. Most sections have recognizable structure, and the reader can follow the broad argument from introduction to conclusion. However, there are frequent issues with phrasing, grammar, punctuation, and APA consistency. Some sentences are awkward or imprecise, and there are several wording problems such as inconsistent terminology, duplicated ideas, and occasional vague formulations. There are also notable formatting inconsistencies in citations and references, spacing issues, and some sentences that reduce clarity. The structure is mostly clear, but not polished. This places the paper in the developing-to-adequate range; because the content remains understandable, the score stays passing but below average.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is detailed and useful, but it mixes several dimensions that can vary independently, such as grammar, paragraph structure, APA accuracy, and vagueness. In practice, this can make holistic grading harder when a paper is strong in structure but weak in APA, or vice versa. It may help to provide brief weighting guidance or examples of what kinds of language issues should meaningfully lower the grade at this course level.

intro_feedback: The Introduction presents a clear topic, establishes societal relevance, defines key concepts, and ends with a clear research aim and hypothesis. The overall line of reasoning is coherent and appropriate for this course level. A strength is that the student attempts to build an argument from broader social relevance to VRET, then to self-guided VRET, and finally to self-efficacy as a possible explanatory mechanism. The required core literature is also incorporated. However, the argument is not fully convincing throughout. Some claims are too speculative or loosely connected, especially the leap from digitalization to increased social anxiety and from autonomy to improved treatment outcome via self-efficacy. The literature review is partly synthetic, but often still reads as sequential summary rather than tightly connected building blocks. In addition, the comparison with the required studies is somewhat imprecise: Anderson, Kampmann, and Bouchard are mentioned, but their exact relevance to the proposed design is not always accurately described. The theoretical framework is present, but it is not fully developed into a strong justification for why self-guided VRET should outperform therapist-guided VRET specifically. Overall, this is above average for level, with a clear research question and a reasonably coherent argument, but not yet strongly argued enough for a higher grade.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric captures the core priorities well by emphasizing line of reasoning, scientific relevance, clarity of the RQ, and responsible use of references. A useful improvement would be to distinguish more explicitly between literature summary and literature synthesis, because many student papers are not incoherent but still weak in integrating studies into one argument. It may also help to mention alignment between theory, prior research, and the proposed design more directly, since this is central in the writing guide but only implicit in the rubric.
methods_feedback: The Method section describes a coherent three-group design that matches the stated research question reasonably well. Participants, materials, and procedure are all present, and the reader can broadly understand what was done. Basic demographics, recruitment, random assignment, reward, and inclusion criteria are reported, which supports an adequate score. However, there are several important weaknesses that prevent a higher grade. The description is incomplete in places: exclusion criteria are not fully operationalized, allocation is described vaguely as 'AI (coinflip),' and there is no clear explanation of how randomization was implemented. The intervention descriptions are uneven and not well standardized across conditions. The self-guided and therapist-guided VRET conditions differ on several dimensions besides guidance, including likely number of sessions, intensity, and setting, which creates confounds that are not acknowledged in the Methods. The LSAS is described only briefly and lacks several details expected in the writing guide, such as example item, score range, and fuller scoring explanation. Procedure and analysis information are also somewhat mixed into other subsections. Finally, saying the analysis 'used statistical analysis (Repeated Measures ANOVA)' is too brief for a fully solid Methods section. Overall, the design is understandable and mostly aligned with the RQ, but important procedural and measurement details are missing or insufficiently controlled.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric appropriately focuses on coherence between design, RQ, and hypotheses, as well as completeness and comprehensibility of participants, materials, and procedures. A limitation is that 'complete and correct' remains somewhat broad. The rubric could be strengthened by explicitly naming key expected elements for this course level, such as allocation procedure, inclusion/exclusion criteria, intervention comparability, measurement detail, and enough procedural information for approximate replication. This would help graders distinguish between nearly complete and genuinely complete methods sections more consistently.
results_feedback: The Results section follows the expected general structure and includes demographic information, outcome means, and the intended main analysis. This helps it reach a minimal passing level. However, the section is substantially incomplete and contains several reporting problems. The tables are referred to but not properly integrated into the section as formatted tables, and the statistics are often incorrectly or incompletely reported. For example, the ANOVA results omit key elements such as degrees of freedom formatting consistency and exact test statistics are presented in a way that does not appear plausible for the reported design. There is also inconsistency in terminology and outcome reporting, such as referring to 'PCL-5 scores' instead of LSAS scores. The post-hoc reporting is not fully coherent: first a significant post-measurement difference is reported, then no significant difference between the two VRET groups is reported, without clearly reconciling which comparisons were significant. The wait-list condition is barely interpreted despite being part of the design. Assumption checking is minimal and incomplete relative to the sample template. Overall, the Results are relevant to the design and partly structured appropriately, but incompleteness and internal inconsistencies make the reporting just sufficient rather than adequate.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric correctly emphasizes whether analyses and reporting are correct, complete, coherent, and relevant to the design. However, the jump between categories could be made more concrete for student-level work. Given the calibration summary and sample results, the rubric would benefit from explicitly including expected components such as demographics table, descriptive statistics table, assumption checks, main analysis, and post-hoc interpretation. That would make grading more transparent and better aligned with the provided sample.
discussion_feedback: The Discussion clearly restates the aim, summarizes the main findings, and addresses whether the hypothesis was supported. It appropriately concludes that both VRET conditions reduced social anxiety symptoms and that the predicted superiority of self-guided VRET was not supported. This makes the core reasoning mostly correct and coherent. A strong point is that the student does try to interpret the unexpected lack of difference between the two active treatments rather than ignoring it. The discussion also includes limitations, future research, and a concluding practical implication. However, the interpretation remains somewhat limited. The links back to theory are present but not deeply developed: self-efficacy is discussed, yet the study did not measure self-efficacy directly, so the theoretical interpretation remains speculative. The integration with prior research is somewhat selective and could be more tightly connected to the exact findings. There is also limited engagement with the wait-list condition, despite it being part of the design and conclusion. Some implications are slightly stronger than the study design and reporting justify. Still, for this level, the section is coherent, relevant, and reasonably argued, though not especially nuanced or complete.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric captures the importance of the main conclusion, coherence of reasoning, relevance of critical reflection, and responsible use of references. It could be improved by making explicit that a strong discussion should not only restate findings but also interpret them in relation to theory, prior literature, limitations, and implications. In its current form, those expectations are somewhat bundled under broad wording, which may reduce grading precision between adequate and good discussions.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally readable and the scientific tone is mostly appropriate for a second-year student paper. The overall structure is clear, with recognizable sections and mostly understandable paragraphing. References are generally used responsibly, and the reader can follow the intended argument. However, there are noticeable issues in phrasing, grammar, punctuation, and APA consistency. Some sentences are awkward or imprecise, and there are occasional wording problems such as inconsistent terminology, repeated phrases, and minor grammatical errors. There are also APA inconsistencies in citation style, formatting of references, punctuation, spacing, and statistical notation. A few statements are vague or overly broad. Still, these issues do not usually impede understanding. Overall, the writing is around adequate to slightly above average: clear enough to communicate the study, but not polished.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is detailed and practical, especially in covering structure, grammar, APA, vagueness, and redundancy. One strength is that it separates clarity from formal correctness. A possible improvement would be to clarify how much APA/statistical formatting errors should weigh relative to readability and scientific clarity, especially since the calibration summary indicates that minor APA issues should not heavily penalize students. More explicit student-level anchors could also help distinguish adequate from good writing.

intro_feedback: The Introduction shows a clear topic, establishes societal relevance, defines key concepts, and ends with a clear research aim and hypothesis. The overall line of reasoning is understandable and generally coherent: digitalization relates to social anxiety, VRET is introduced as a promising intervention, and self-guided VRET is proposed as a potentially valuable extension. The paper also uses references responsibly and includes the required core VRET literature. A clear strength is that the student attempts to build a theoretical rationale around self-efficacy rather than only listing prior findings. However, the argument is only somewhat convincing rather than strongly compelling. The theoretical framework is not fully tight: self-efficacy is presented as central, but the paper does not clearly explain why self-guidance should improve self-efficacy within this specific treatment context strongly enough to outperform therapist guidance. Some supporting citations are only indirectly relevant to the exact comparison being made. In addition, the discussion of the required prior studies is somewhat imprecise: Kampmann is described as individual in-vivo exposure rather than clearly as VR social interaction exposure, and the building-block structure is present but not very sharply synthesized. Overall, this fits the rubric's adequate range: correct and coherent, with a clear relevant RQ, but only somewhat convincingly argued.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric captures the core priority of this course well by focusing on the line of reasoning toward the RQ, relevance, and hypothesis. A possible improvement would be to make literature synthesis more explicit as a criterion, because students can appear coherent while still writing article-by-article summaries. It may also help to specify how much weight should be given to societal relevance versus theoretical relevance, since both are emphasized in the writing guide.
methods_feedback: The Methods section describes a coherent randomized design that generally matches the research question and hypothesis. Participants, basic recruitment, inclusion criteria, conditions, and the broad intervention structure are all present. The section is understandable and mostly complete for this course level. There are also useful concrete details, such as sample size per group, reward, intervention duration, and basic information about the VR setups. However, important methodological details are missing or insufficiently specified. The participant description lacks a reported overall mean age and SD in the main text, and the inclusion/exclusion criteria are not fully justified. Group allocation is described vaguely as 'using AI (coinflip),' which is not an appropriate or precise description of randomization. methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric is useful in emphasizing coherence between design and RQ, but 'complete and correct' remains somewhat broad. results_feedback: The Results section is the weakest part of the paper because the reporting is incomplete and at points inconsistent with the stated design. A strength is that the student follows the expected broad structure: sample description, ANOVA, descriptive tables, and post-hoc statements. However, the section falls short of the sample-results standard in several important ways. results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric appropriately emphasizes correctness, completeness, coherence, and relevance. discussion_feedback: The Discussion contains a clear main conclusion and correctly answers the research question: both active interventions reduced social anxiety symptoms, but self-guided VRET was not superior to therapist-guided VRET. Still, the discussion is not fully developed. The theoretical integration remains somewhat limited: self-efficacy is central in the Introduction, but the Discussion does not deeply evaluate what the null difference implies for that theoretical account or whether the theory should be modified. Some interpretation relies on outside studies that are only indirectly comparable, and the paper does not sufficiently consider design-based alternative explanations such as unequal treatment dosage or the lack of direct self-efficacy measurement. discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric correctly prioritizes reasoning toward a main conclusion and critical reflection. A useful refinement would be to explicitly mention integration with prior literature and theory, because this is central in the writing guide and calibration summary. It may also help to distinguish more clearly between merely restating results and actually interpreting them, since this is a common student difficulty.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally readable and uses mostly appropriate scientific language. The structure across sections is clear, and most paragraphs have a recognizable focus. lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is detailed and helpful, especially because it includes structure, ambiguity, redundancy, and APA. One possible improvement is to clarify how heavily APA/reference-list errors should count relative to clarity and argumentation at this course level. intro_feedback:

In addition, there are some inaccuracies or weaker links in the reasoning: for example, the descriptions of the core studies are not always precise, and the jump from autonomy/self-guidance to higher self-efficacy and then to superior symptom reduction is plausible but not strongly established with direct evidence in this exact context. The societal relevance paragraph is present and relevant, but somewhat broad and not always tightly tied to the specific design choice of comparing self-guided versus therapist-guided VRET. Overall, the Introduction fits the 'good' range: coherent, mostly sound, and clearly leading to the RQ and hypothesis, but with some weaker argumentative links.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric captures the course emphasis on argumentation well, especially the distinction between merely reviewing studies and actually using them to build toward a research question. A possible refinement would be to separate 'coverage of required components' from 'quality of synthesis' more explicitly, because a paper can include all required elements yet still have weak argumentative integration. It may also help to operationalize what counts as a sufficiently developed theoretical framework for this assignment level, since students are beginners and may not always know how much theory is enough.
methods_feedback:

The Participants, Materials, and Procedure subsections are all present, and the reader can broadly understand what was done. Important elements such as recruitment source, random assignment, inclusion criteria, reward, intervention duration, and the main outcome measure are included. For this student level, the overall design is understandable and mostly aligned with the paper’s aims.

However, multiple important details are missing or underdeveloped, which keeps the section in the adequate rather than good range. Participant information is incomplete: the overall sample size and group sizes are given, but demographic details such as mean age and gender distribution are not properly integrated into the Participants section itself. The therapist-guided condition is less fully specified than the self-guided condition in terms of exact session content and standardization. The wait-list condition is barely described beyond not receiving treatment. The LSAS description is too brief and misses several elements recommended in the writing guide, such as response format details, score range, and an example item. There is also some misplaced content, such as mention of the statistical analysis in the Procedure section and procedural phrasing inside Materials. Finally, the phrase 'using AI (coinflip)' is inappropriate and unclear as a description of allocation. Overall, the method is coherent and mostly complete, but it lacks one to several details that matter for replication and clarity.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric is clear in emphasizing coherence, completeness, and correct placement of information. A useful improvement would be to specify a minimal checklist of details expected for Participants, Materials, Procedure, and Analysis, because the current wording leaves some room for subjective interpretation of what counts as an 'important detail.' It could also more explicitly distinguish between minor omissions and omissions that meaningfully reduce replicability.
results_feedback:
The Results section includes the basic intended structure: opening statement about the analyzed sample, mention of outliers, an inferential test, post-hoc interpretation, and references to tables and a figure. The demographic and outcome values are provided at the end of the paper, so the necessary descriptive information is in the submission. There is also an attempt to report the interaction and to interpret the treatment pattern across conditions.

However, this section has substantial reporting problems relative to the rubric and sample. The tables are not actually presented in the Results section in a clear, formatted way where they are introduced, and the figure is only named without content. Statistical reporting is incomplete and at points incorrect or internally inconsistent: several test statistics are missing commas/equal signs/df formatting, the reported degrees of freedom look implausible for the stated design, and the section states both that the post-treatment difference was significant with therapist-guided VRET showing the biggest reduction and also that there was no significant difference between self-guided and therapist-guided VRET at post-assessment. The outcome label also shifts to 'PCL-5 scores' once, which is incorrect for this study. Assumption checks are minimal and incomplete, and the reporting does not fully match the sample expectations for this course. Because the core structure is attempted and some relevant analyses are reported, this reaches the lower passing/developing range, but the inaccuracies and incompleteness prevent a higher score.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric benefits from the concrete link to the sample results, which gives students and graders a useful benchmark. Still, the criteria could be more explicit about how to weigh different kinds of problems: missing tables/figures, incorrect statistical notation, contradictory interpretation, and mismatch between stated design and reported analysis do not all have the same severity. A slightly more analytic breakdown within Results could improve consistency across graders.
discussion_feedback:
The Discussion clearly restates the study aim, addresses the main findings, and explicitly evaluates whether the hypothesis was supported. It also compares the results to previous literature and offers an explanation for the unexpected lack of superiority of self-guided VRET. The student does more than merely repeat the results: they interpret the null difference between active treatments and propose that therapist support may offset autonomy-related advantages. The section also includes study-specific limitations and future research suggestions, which are relevant and mostly grounded in the design.

At the same time, the discussion is not fully strong in linking the findings back to the theoretical framework in a deep way. The self-efficacy explanation remains somewhat speculative because self-efficacy was never measured, so the theory is invoked more as a post hoc frame than as a directly tested mechanism. The comparison to prior research is present but sometimes somewhat list-like or broad, and the discussion could have engaged more explicitly with the wait-list findings and with the exact pattern shown in the data. There is also some redundancy, as the same main finding is stated several times before being developed further. Still, the section is mostly coherent, study-specific, and reasonably well connected to the Introduction, which places it in the adequate-to-good range.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric appropriately prioritizes interpretation, integration with theory, critical reflection, and implications. One way to strengthen it would be to distinguish more clearly between a discussion that merely mentions theory and one that genuinely uses theory to interpret findings or revise expectations. It may also help to include clearer guidance on how to judge discussions of unsupported hypotheses, since this is a common challenge for students and an important indicator of scientific reasoning.
lang_style_feedback:
The paper is generally readable and uses scientific language appropriately for this course level. Terminology is mostly consistent, and the overall structure of the paper is clear, with recognizable subsections and a conventional research-paper flow. Most sentences are understandable, and the main argument can be followed without major difficulty.

There are, however, several language and APA issues that prevent a higher score. Some sentences are awkwardly phrased or grammatically off, punctuation and spacing are inconsistent, citation formatting is uneven, and there are noticeable style inconsistencies in references and in-text citations. There is also some redundancy and occasional imprecision in wording. A few wording choices reduce formality or clarity, such as 'using AI (coinflip)' and informal phrasing in methods/procedure. These issues do not seriously impede understanding, but they are frequent enough to keep the score in the adequate range rather than good.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is practical and appropriately prevents graders from over-penalizing content scores for writing problems. However, counting grammar, APA, or vague-statement errors can be difficult in practice and may reduce inter-rater consistency unless graders apply it loosely. The rubric might work better if it emphasized overall readability, structural clarity, and consistency of terminology slightly more than approximate error counts.

intro_feedback:
The Introduction presents a clear research topic, societal relevance, a recognizable theoretical angle, and a concrete research question with hypothesis. It also includes the required core studies and an additional article tailored to the specific focus on self-guided VRET, which supports an overall coherent line of reasoning. The strongest aspect is that the paper does move beyond pure summary in several places: the student uses prior work to argue for a gap, namely the lack of direct comparison between self-guided and therapist-guided VRET. The hypothesis is explicitly stated and generally follows from the argument.

At the same time, the argumentative chain is not consistently strong enough for a higher score. Some links are somewhat speculative or weakly supported. In particular, the move from self-guidance to higher self-efficacy to superior treatment outcomes is plausible, but not sufficiently built up with direct evidence in the specific context of VRET for social anxiety. The theory section relies heavily on broad claims about autonomy and self-efficacy without fully integrating them into a more precise framework explaining why symptom reduction should be greater rather than simply comparable. In addition, some of the discussion of earlier studies is more descriptive than synthetic, and the descriptions of the core articles are not always fully accurate in how they are characterized. The societal relevance paragraph is present and appropriate, but the opening framing around digitalization and declining face-to-face interaction is somewhat broad and not always tightly connected to the specific study design. Overall, this fits the good range: coherent, relevant, and clearly leading to the RQ, but with a few weaker argumentative steps.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric is strong in emphasizing line of reasoning, synthesis, and the connection between prior research and the RQ. A useful refinement would be to make the distinction between 'describing studies' and 'using studies as building blocks' even more operational, perhaps with short observable indicators. It may also help to specify how to judge partially accurate use of the required core articles, since students may include them all but characterize them somewhat imprecisely. Finally, the rubric could clarify how much weight should be given to the societal relevance paragraph relative to theory and literature synthesis when these differ in quality.
methods_feedback:
The Methods section describes a coherent three-group design that is related to the research question and hypotheses. The main components—participants, materials, and procedure—are all present, and the basic design can be understood. Random assignment, the inclusion criterion based on LSAS, the presence of a waitlist control, and broad descriptions of both VRET conditions are all helpful. This places the section above a merely developing level.

However, there are enough important missing or unclear details to keep the grade in the adequate range. Participant information is incomplete: the overall sample size and group sizes are given, but key descriptive details expected in the Methods section itself, such as mean age and gender distribution per condition, are not properly integrated there and instead effectively appear later outside the section. Inclusion and exclusion criteria are partly unclear or awkwardly phrased, especially the exclusion of any prior history or diagnosis of anxiety or depressive disorders while simultaneously requiring high social anxiety. Materials are described only partially: for the LSAS, there is no example item, no scoring range, and no cut-off justification beyond eligibility. The therapist-guided and self-guided interventions are not described at a comparable level of detail, making replication harder. Procedure also lacks precision about timing of pre/post assessment, where assessments were completed, and how adherence was monitored in the self-guided condition. The phrase 'using AI (coinflip)' for randomization is also not appropriate or sufficiently clear as a methodological description. Finally, the analysis plan is placed in the Procedure and remains very brief. So the section is coherent and mostly complete, but it lacks several important details expected by the writing guide.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric gives appropriate attention to coherence, completeness, and whether information is placed in the correct subsection. A possible improvement would be to make the minimum expected details more explicit in the rubric itself rather than relying mainly on the writing guide. For example, separate mention of allocation procedure, timing of measurements, adherence/implementation details, and questionnaire scoring information would make grading more transparent and consistent across assessors. It might also be useful to distinguish more clearly between minor omissions and omissions that directly impair replicability.
results_feedback:
The Results section contains the basic intended analysis and does include some core elements such as a demographics table, outcome means per condition and timepoint, mention of assumption checking, the omnibus ANOVA, post-hoc comparisons, and a figure reference. That is enough to keep it at the lower passing boundary rather than insufficient.

Still, this section is substantially weaker than the sample standard and falls in the developing range. The biggest problem is incompleteness and inconsistency in reporting. Table 1 and Table 2 are referenced in the narrative, but in the body of the Results section they are not properly formatted or embedded as expected; the actual values are only provided at the very end of the paper. The ANOVA statistics are reported incorrectly or at least implausibly/incompletely: F-values are missing commas and degrees of freedom formatting is inconsistent, and the reported dfs do not match the described repeated-measures design clearly. There are no exact p-values where expected. Important assumptions beyond normality are not addressed. The waitlist condition is barely discussed in the post-hoc interpretation, despite being one of the three conditions. There is also internal inconsistency: one sentence states a significant post-measurement difference between conditions with therapist-guided showing the biggest reduction, while the next sentence says there was no significant difference between self-guided and therapist-guided VRET at post-assessment; these could both be true if the waitlist drove the omnibus difference, but this is not clearly explained. In addition, the text mistakenly refers to PCL-5 scores instead of LSAS scores, suggesting reporting was not carefully adapted to the actual study. Overall, the section is relevant and somewhat correct, but incomplete and not clearly aligned with the sample results standard.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric is helpful because it anchors expectations to the sample results and specifies key required elements. A refinement could be to distinguish more clearly between errors in statistical formatting and deeper problems in statistical reasoning or design-reporting mismatch. Right now, 'somewhat correct and complete' versus 'mostly correct and complete' can still leave considerable assessor discretion. It may also help to explicitly include interpretation of all conditions/timepoints as a criterion, since students may report omnibus tests but neglect one group or key comparison.
discussion_feedback:
The Discussion provides a clear main conclusion, answers the research question, and states that the hypothesis was not supported. It also meaningfully distinguishes between what was expected and what was actually found. The student relates the findings back to several studies from the Introduction and attempts to explain the null difference between self-guided and therapist-guided VRET rather than ignoring it. The limitations are study-specific rather than purely generic, especially regarding the student sample and variability in adherence in the self-guided condition. Future research suggestions follow logically from these limitations.

The main reason the grade does not move higher is that the discussion is only partly developed at the theoretical level. Although self-efficacy was central in the Introduction, the Discussion does not really evaluate whether the data support, contradict, or require revision of that theoretical account beyond stating that the expected superiority was not found. Since self-efficacy itself was not measured, this should have been more explicitly acknowledged as an untested mechanism. The interpretation of why therapist guidance may compensate for autonomy is reasonable, but it relies on external analogies more than on a close analysis of this specific design. The waitlist condition is also mentioned mainly in the conclusion rather than integrated throughout the interpretive discussion. Some broader implications are present, but they remain relatively brief and could have tied back more explicitly to the societal relevance developed in the Introduction. Overall, this is a mostly coherent and correct discussion with relevant limitations and interpretation, but not yet fully strong in theory integration.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric appropriately prioritizes interpretation, linkage to the introduction, and study-specific critical reflection. It could be improved by making explicit that discussion of theoretical implications includes evaluating untested mechanisms, not just restating the theory. Another useful addition would be a clearer indicator for how to judge broader implications: for example, whether implications are proportionate to the study design and limitations. This would help distinguish discussions that are coherent but somewhat surface-level from those that are truly strong in integrative reasoning.
lang_style_feedback:
The paper is generally readable, uses mostly appropriate scientific language, and is organized into recognizable sections and paragraphs. Terminology is usually understandable, and the reader can follow the overall argument without major difficulty. This supports an adequate to slightly above adequate score.

There are, however, several noticeable writing and APA issues that prevent a higher grade. Terminology is not always fully consistent: the paper alternates between SA and SAD somewhat loosely, and 'therapy-guided' versus 'therapist-guided' is inconsistent. APA style contains multiple errors in in-text citations, reference formatting, capitalization, spacing, and presentation of tables/figures. Some redundancy is present, particularly in the Discussion where similar conclusions are repeated across adjacent paragraphs. None of this seriously obscures meaning, but there are too many issues for the language and style to be considered nearly faultless.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is generally clear and appropriately prevents over-penalizing content for language issues. One improvement would be to separate APA/reference accuracy from prose quality a bit more explicitly, since these can differ substantially and may currently be bundled too broadly. In addition, the counts of grammar or APA errors are practical in principle, but in real grading they can be difficult to apply consistently; more qualitative anchor examples for each band could improve reliability. The rubric might also explicitly mention consistency between tables, figures, and text as part of style/presentation.
